idiom_name: struct itinerary of function pointers in the message header + dispatch loop
implementation_notes: C has no message abstraction and no closures, so the slip is a plain data structure: an ordered array of step functions (int (*step)(struct msg *)) plus a cursor index carried in the message header, with a small dispatch loop that calls the current entry and increments the cursor. That function-pointer table IS the classic Router/Step structure reduced to its minimum - there is no framework that can absorb it, so the hand-written form is the normal one. Where steps need per-step configuration or state, extend the entry with a void *ctx (or an index into a configuration table) instead of inventing an object hierarchy; a virtual-method emulation is only worth it when steps are polymorphic at runtime.
pitfalls: A fixed-size itinerary array needs a bound on slip length; otherwise allocate it dynamically with one clearly defined owner and free path, or the header leaks.
Function pointers carry no state, so per-step context must travel explicitly (void *ctx, step index, or a config table); a static/global context silently breaks concurrent messages.
Every step returns int, so partial completion is invisible unless each step's failure path is written down: arrange idempotency or an undo hook, and never ignore a non-zero return in the loop.
Shared itinerary buffers must not be mutated by concurrent messages: copy the slip per message or treat it as read-only.
